title: The problem of self-consistent particle phase space distributions for periodic focusing channels
abstract: Charged particle beams in equilibrium with their collective fields are represented by self-consistent phase space distributions. As the starting point, we assume the external focusing forces to act continuously on the beam. In the collisionless mean-field approximation, a broad class of stationary self-consistent particle phase space distributions can then be constructed. The method is reviewed how to determine the single-particle Hamiltonian of the focusing system for a given phase space density function. Subsequently, canonical transformations are used to relate this description to a beam passing through a non-continuous transport system. The correspondence is exact for the linear K-V model and provides an approximate matching prescription for distributions with nonlinear space-charge forces. The transverse Hamiltonian generally changes with the focusing strength, including in a rotationally symmetric periodic solenoid channel. Our computer simulations, presented in the second part of the paper, indicate very small rms-emittance changes for appropriately matched beams in the continuous and periodic solenoid channels investigated. The simulation for a periodic quadrupole channel yields a small persistent increase of the rms-emittance, whose physical interpretation requires control of numerical errors.   Revised version of: Particle~Accelerators 39, 219--249 (1992)}

title: Improved envelope and emittance description of particle beams using the Fokker-Planck approach
abstract: Beam dynamics calculations based on the collisionless Vlasov equation omit collisional correlations such as intra-beam scattering. For a short-correlated process dominated by small momentum changes, a Fokker-Planck equation can describe their effect on the one-particle distribution. From this equation we derive equations of motion for the beam envelopes and for the rms-emittances. Prescribed friction against an external bath is distinguished from momentum- and energy-conserving self-collisions. For the latter, an affine mean-flow approximation and a scalar relaxation coefficient give simple equations for temperature balancing within the beam. The longitudinal diffusion and temperature are expressed in terms of the physical random momentum rather than the signed effective longitudinal mass. The resulting growth-rate formulas apply to this reduced relaxation model. The original numerical examples are retained for comparison, with the limitations of the storage-ring and numerical-noise applications made explicit. Revised version of: Particle Accelerators~{\bf 45}, 229 (1994)

title: On the stability and emittance growth of different particle phase-space distributions in a long magnetic quadrupole channel
abstract: The behavior of K-V, waterbag, parabolic, conical and Gaussian distributions in periodic quadrupole channels is studied by particle simulations. In the parameter range studied, the response associated with the K-V instabilities becomes progressively less pronounced toward the Gaussian distribution. For the third-order instability studied here, the emittance growth factor of an initially Gaussian beam after a large number of periods is considerably lower than that of an equivalent K-V distribution.\newline\indent In addition, the non-K-V distributions exhibit a rapid initial emittance growth within approximately one period of the channel, which becomes very significant at high beam intensities. This growth is attributed to the homogenization of the space-charge density, resulting in a conversion of electric-field energy into transverse kinetic and potential energy. Two simple analytical formulae based on different energy-partition assumptions are derived as estimates for this effect and are compared with the results obtained from particle simulations. They are not rigorous lower and upper bounds for arbitrary beam evolution. \\[6pt] Revised version of: Particle Accelerators {\bf 15}, 47--65 (1984)}

title: Theoretical studies of envelope oscillations and instabilities of mismatched intense charged-particle beams in periodic focusing channels
abstract: The behavior of mismatched intense charged-particle beams in periodic transport channels of the solenoid and quadrupole type is studied theoretically. The envelope-oscillation frequencies of the mismatched beam are obtained by the smooth-approximation method and by numerical evaluation of the linearly perturbed K-V envelope equations. Phase shifts of the envelope oscillations and growth factors per focusing period in the case of instability are calculated for a solenoid and a magnetic quadrupole (FODO) channel using the parameters of the Maryland and GSI beam transport experiments. For comparison and the purpose of illustration, the K-V equations are integrated numerically, and envelope curves as well as single-particle trajectories for mismatched beams are shown in graphical form. In addition, computer simulation studies with the PARMILA code were performed, and results are presented both for K-V and a Gaussian distribution in transverse phase space.\\~\\ Revised version of: Particle~Accelerators~{\bf 14}, 227--260 (1984)}

title: In-situ azimuthal sample rotation within a horizontal-field cryomagnet for small-angle neutron scattering
abstract: We present an in-situ azimuthal rotation stage for small-angle neutron scattering measurements. The stage provides an azimuthal rotation range of $315^\circ$ about the stage normal. At the reference sample-stick orientation, the stage normal is parallel to the incident neutron beam, so that the sample rotates in the plane perpendicular to the beam. Combined with a sample stick rotation about a second, orthogonal axis, the stage provides control of the magnetic-field direction relative to the crystal axes, while the field remains fixed in the laboratory frame. For a 5 mm diameter incident beam, sample-stick rotations of approximately $\pm315^\circ$ are accessible with negligible additional attenuation from the holder. The commercial rotator is specified for operation between 1 and 373 K and in magnetic fields up to 35 T, making the stage nominally compatible with the full temperature (1.8 to 320 K) and field (0 to 6.8 T) ranges of the used cryomagnet. As a working example, we characterize its performance on a spherical single crystal of MnSi between 20 and 35 K and in fields up to 183 mT, observing local sample heating during operation of $\sim$20 mK per $5^\circ$ step. We illustrate the design considerations behind the holder construction, with specific notes for mounting spherical samples, and discuss the resulting performance and limitations.

title: Plasma waveguides for high-intensity laser pulses
abstract: Fundamental to many applications of laser pulses in science and technology is an extended interaction length with matter that significantly exceeds the distance over which the pulse would normally diffract and transversely spread. At low intensity, the interaction could simply be the linear refraction provided by a glass optical fiber to keep the pulse from spreading. At higher pulse intensities, however, the goal extends beyond diffraction-free pulse transport: an extended interaction length of high intensity light can give rise to bright secondary sources of photons and, at relativistic intensities, beams of high energy charged particles. Since these applications require laser intensities well above the threshold for ionization of atoms, new methods for overcoming pulse diffraction in a plasma have been developed. Chief among them are plasma waveguides -- optical fibers composed of plasma, with characteristic mode structure. This article reviews the methods and theory of plasma waveguides, highlighting the recent development of meter-scale plasma waveguides that have been instrumental to the laser acceleration of high-charge electron beams to energies ~10 GeV

title: Polarized quantum effects in countable signals from intense laser - electron beam interactions
abstract: We investigate the feasibility of precision counting experiments in laser-electron-beam collisions for testing strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED), with particular emphasis on spin-dependent effects. To resolve such rare signals, we develop a high-precision Monte Carlo model combining spin- and polarization-resolved QED rates with weighted photon packets, hierarchical-mesh sampling, and adaptive time stepping. The model is quantitatively benchmarked against the high-energy edge of the photon spectrum and the positron yield in the SLAC E-144 experiment. The high-energy photon spectrum and total positron yield are only weakly affected by spin-dependent corrections, even at higher laser intensities. In contrast, we find that spin asymmetry in photon emission significantly affects the polarization of photons in the high-energy tail, while spin asymmetry in pair production manifests itself as a spin-dependent imbalance in the large-angle positron population. These microscopic spin asymmetries give rise to experimentally countable signals through their correlations with the oscillating laser field. Our predictions could be tested using moderate-energy electron beams and optical lasers with intensities of approximately 10^22 W/cm2, as envisaged in future ELI-NP experiments.

title: Hydrogen and Lithium Isotope Analysis via Optical Spectroscopy of Laser-Produced Plasmas
abstract: Accurate detection and quantification of light-element isotopes, particularly hydrogen (H) and lithium (Li), are essential across chemistry, materials science, geology, nuclear energy, forensics, and defense applications. Their isotopic compositions provide insight into fuel cycles, materials degradation, mass transport, and environmental processes. Hydrogen and Li isotopes are especially relevant in nuclear environments because neutron-induced reactions directly connect their isotopic inventories. Despite their importance, analysis of these light isotopes remains challenging due to their low atomic mass, high mobility, and, in some cases, radiological constraints. While some existing analytical techniques can detect and measure H and/or Li, they typically require extensive sample preparation, laboratory-based instrumentation, or extended analysis times that preclude real-time monitoring capabilities. To address these limitations, optical spectroscopy of laser-produced plasmas offers a promising solution, enabling field-deployable, standoff sensing of isotopic signatures with real-time analysis capability and no sample preparation requirement. This Topical Review summarizes fundamentals and recent advances in H and Li isotopic analysis using optical spectroscopy, with emphasis on laser-produced plasmas generated by laser ablation of solid targets. Key concepts relevant to isotope-resolved optical measurements are introduced, including isotope shifts, fine and hyperfine structure, and line-broadening mechanisms. Progress in optical emission, laser induced fluorescence, and absorption spectroscopy is reviewed for H and Li isotopes.

title: Modeling runaway electron mitigation via passively driven plasma instabilities in a high-current tokamak
abstract: A critical challenge for tokamak-based fusion power plants is the formation of high-current, relativistic runaway electron (RE) beams during abrupt confinement loss events called disruptions. RE beams may significantly damage machine components if left unmitigated, jeopardizing the operational and economic viability of fusion power plants. We present the first self-consistent extended magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) computational study of RE mitigation with a passively driven RE mitigation coil (REMC) in a high-current tokamak. RE generation and transport are coupled with REMC-driven MHD activity in a 3D simulation that models the thermal and current quench phases of a mid-plane disruption, together with the vertical displacement and final termination of the plasma and RE beam on SPARC -- a high-field, high-current tokamak designed to achieve a fusion gain Q > 1. We demonstrate that REMC-driven magnetic stochasticity can reduce the RE current by over an order-of-magnitude when compared to unmitigated disruptions. The final termination is mediated via a post-thermal-quench "cold" vertical displacement of the plasma, which, together with magnetic stochasticity, increases RE losses via scrape-off once the plasma contacts the first wall. These results demonstrate a viable mechanism for RE mitigation using passively driven plasma instabilities on high-current tokamaks.

title: Residual AM and PM Noise of Selected X-Band Amplifiers
abstract: In microwave systems design, amplitude modulation (AM) noise is often ignored relative to phase modulation (PM) noise. However, in high-performance applications requiring ultra-low PM noise, AM noise becomes a critical limiting factor due to AM-to-PM conversion mechanisms. Because AM noise specifications are rarely, if ever, provided for commercial microwave components, this study characterizes the residual AM and PM noise of several 10 GHz amplifiers. We present performance data for various Heterojunction Bipolar Transistor (HBT) amplifier designs and demonstrate the noise reduction achieved through power-summed configurations. For example, a discrete-die GaAs HBT amplifier achieves residual PM noise below $-160$ dBrad$^2$/Hz and AM noise of approximately $-155$ dB/Hz at a 1 kHz offset in a quad power-summed configuration. A notable finding is that the majority of amplifier designs surveyed in this study exhibit higher AM noise relative to their PM noise, with only a few exceptions. The impact of bias supply quality on residual noise is also quantified, demonstrating that the choice of voltage regulator is a first-order design parameter below 1 kHz offset.

title: Eddy currents and error fields in the toroidally segmented shell configuration aka Armadillo
abstract: A stream function formulation for the calculation of the eddy current distribution in a toroidally segmented conducting shell (Armadillo) is presented and verified. The governing Poisson-like equation is solved spectrally via a Discrete Sine Transform, which enforces the zero-current boundary condition at each gap exactly by construction, and the related radial magnetic field at the plasma surface is obtained by Biot-Savart integration. The toroidal eddy current flows in the same direction on every sector with a cosine-like poloidal distribution, while the poloidal return current, required by current continuity, peaks near each gap and reverses sign between adjacent sectors. The scaling of both components with the number of gaps is governed by the competition between the poloidal geometric scale of the shell and the toroidal segmentation scale. The transition between the two regimes is set by the aspect ratio of the device, around eight gaps for an RFX-mod2-like geometry, as predicted by the analytical wall time model of the Armadillo configuration. At the gap, the poloidal return current produces a radial field of opposite sign to the value far from the gap; the resulting non-axisymmetric error field peaks near this transition and becomes negligible for highly segmented shells. These results provide a first characterisation of the eddy currents and error fields of the Armadillo configuration, needed for future resistive wall mode and tearing mode stability analyses.

title: Positron Emission Tomography with quantum-entangled Compton events: first imaging results at clinically relevant activities
abstract: In Positron Emission Tomography, a potential, yet unutilized enhancement, may come from exploiting the quantum entanglement of the annihilation quanta, inscribed in the correlation of their polarizations. To investigate this, we built a PET demonstrator capable of measuring polarization correlations of annihilation quanta by their Compton scattering, based on single-layer scintillator polarimeters. We present a detailed study of the imaging of two $^{68}$Ge line sources, 45 MBq each, to extract the spatial resolution and assess image quality. The results show that a spatial resolution of 2.5$\pm$0.1 mm is obtained using single-pixel events, while resolutions obtained with polarization-correlated Compton events range from 3.6$\pm$0.3 mm to 4.9$\pm$0.3 mm, depending on data selection criteria. We also found that the polarization-correlated Compton events exhibit up to 20% higher average signal to random background ratio compared to the single-pixel events. We also present the first imaging of the NEMA NU-4 phantom filled with a $^{68}$Ga solution of 378 MBq initial activity, successfully combining polarization-correlated events with conventional single-pixel event selection. Based on the extracted spatial resolution, signal-to-background, signal-to-noise, contrast, and contrast-to-noise ratio, we estimate that up to 10% sensitivity increase may be attained by exploiting the polarization-correlated events, while preserving a high image quality.

title: Design of a radio-frequency photoinjector for generating relativistic vortex electron beams
abstract: We present the design and an analysis of the classical and quantum beam dynamics for an S-band radio-frequency (RF) photoinjector dedicated to the generation of relativistic vortex electron beams carrying a quantized orbital angular momentum (OAM). The field-map-based tracking simulations were performed in the ultra-low bunch charge regime ($Q = 0.63$ pC), where space-charge effects are strongly suppressed. We demonstrate that optimizing the injection phase and solenoidal focusing preserves the intrinsic thermal limit of the photoemission source, yielding a stable, emittance-compensated beam with a final kinetic energy of 4.9 MeV and a normalized transverse emittance of $56\,π\,μ\mathrm{m}\cdot\mathrm{mrad}$. Furthermore, our quantum-mechanical analysis of single-electron Laguerre-Gaussian wave packets inside the designed accelerating fields reveals that rapid energy gain suppresses transverse quantum spreading by nearly three orders of magnitude compared to free-space propagation. This suppression protects the characteristic OAM-dependent spatial structure of the wave packet. These results establish the beam-dynamics operating regime and vacuum conditions required for subsequent experiments on the generation and transport of relativistic vortex electron beams.

title: Non-Maxwellianity in Temperature Relaxation between Plasma Species
abstract: Temperature relaxation between plasma species is usually described by Landau--Spitzer (LS) theory, which assumes Maxwellian distributions throughout. We show analytically that, for two Maxwellian species in homogeneous isotropic plasmas, the interspecies collisions driving relaxation generate a universal three-lobe initial distortion and that these distortions initially reduce energy exchange over a broad parameter range. Full Fokker--Planck simulations reveal substantial relaxation delays when interspecies deformation competes with self-thermalization. For post-shock deuterium--tritium plasmas relevant to inertial confinement fusion, with $T_{\mathrm{T}}/T_{\mathrm{D}}=1.5$, the relaxation time exceeds the LS prediction by 47%. The accompanying distortions lower the apparent DD/DT temperature ratio and produce positive DD and negative DT Gamow-shift residuals relative to Maxwellian predictions. These results also motivate examining non-Maxwellianity in fuel heating by fusion $α$ particles.

title: The preplasma origin of the plasma-mirror reflectivity response
abstract: Plasma mirrors (PM) enhance the temporal contrast of high-power lasers, but declining reflectivity at subrelativistic intensities limits their energy throughput. Here we show that prepulse-generated preplasma drives this decline in p polarization primarily through absorption. Particle-in-cell simulations using a measured prepulse profile reproduce the reflectivity decrease, with near- and far-field energy accounting showing a weak contribution from scattering. Optical-cycle-resolved electron tracking reveals successive electron bunches extracted from the plasma surface, supporting a vacuum-heating interpretation. Under the simulated conditions, s-polarized absorption remains weak and no comparable decline occurs. Applying the model to two representative double-plasma-mirror (DPM) systems, BELLA and CoReLS, it captures both the p-polarized and s-polarized reflectivity responses across the operating range. Yet, the model still misses the high-fluence s-polarized reflectivity rollover, and further investigation of the scattering channel might be needed. These findings connect prepulse history to polarization-dependent energy loss, informing the choice of plasma-mirror operating conditions.

title: Characterization of immersed SiPM arrays in liquid scintillator between room temperature and $-30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$
abstract: Liquid scintillator detectors instrumented with distributed silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays can be used in compact, topology-sensitive, and low-background experiments, but the temperature dependence of SiPMs immersed directly in the scintillation medium has not been widely characterized. We report the operation of a 125-liter linear-alkylbenzene-based liquid scintillator detector read out by 125 SiPM channels immersed in the active volume, over the range from room temperature to $-30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The detector response was measured with cosmic-ray muons, including stopping muons followed by their Michel-electron decay. Cooling from $+15\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $-30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ reduced the SiPM dark-count rate by a factor of 13.5, increased the single-photoelectron response by 49.1%, and increased the cosmic-ray muon light yield by 16.7%. The improved photoelectron separation and baseline stability at low temperature enabled a selection of stopping-muon events, from which the effective muon lifetime was measured to be $1959\pm132\,\mathrm{ns}$, consistent with the value expected for a hydrocarbon scintillator once $μ^{-}$ capture on carbon is taken into account.

title: Conceptual Design of Pumping Systems up to 1000 m3/s Based on Non-Evaporable Getters in a Gas-Dynamic Magnetic Trap
abstract: The Gas-Dynamic Magnetic Trap (GDMT), a new linear magnetic facility for confining high-temperature hydrogen plasma, is currently under development at the Budker Institute of Nuclear Physics (BINP SB RAS). The total hydrogen flow that must be removed from the end expanders by the vacuum system is approximately 10^22 molecules/s, which corresponds to a required pumping speed on the order of 500 m3/s. Non-evaporable getters (NEG) are considered as a possible pumping method for this application. This article presents experimental studies of Ti-Zr-Al getters manufactured by Polema LLC. The pumping speed, sorption capacity, and sticking factors of the getter surface were measured. The sticking factors for hydrogen and deuterium are 2.23% and 1.54%, respectively. The getter pumping speed is maintained over 60 air-vent/reactivation cycles. Based on these results, a conceptual design of a NEG-based pumping system for the GDMT end expanders is proposed, providing a specific pumping speed of 74 m3/(m3s) for the getter panel. The proposed pumping system design and the required heating power are discussed.

title: High-Efficiency Wakefield Acceleration of Positrons via a Slit Plasma Channel
abstract: Although plasma-based wakefield acceleration has achieved remarkable success for electrons, efficient positron acceleration remains a long standing challenge, as positrons suffer severe defocusing in the accelerating phases of such structures. Here, we propose a slit plasma wakefield acceleration (SPWA) scheme, in which a relativistic electron beam propagating through a slit channel formed by two parallel plasma slabs excites crossing plasma-electron filamentary structures within the slit, generating intense wakefields tailored to simultaneously provide longitudinal acceleration and transverse focusing for a trailing positron bunch. A theoretical model is developed to characterize the wakefield structure responsible for positron acceleration and focusing. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations validate the model, and demonstrate that the SPWA scheme achieves a positron trapping efficiency of nearly 100%, while maintaining low emittance growth and narrow energy spread for an injected positron beam. These findings establish a new and robust approach to high-efficiency positron acceleration, with promising implications for future compact electron-positron colliders and high-energy positron applications.

title: A Two-Dimensional Physics-Informed Neural Network Model of a Hall Effect Thruster Plasma: Self-Consistent Electrostatics and Physical-Consistency Diagnostics
abstract: We present a two-dimensional axisymmetric physics-informed neural network (PINN) of the discharge channel of the P5 Hall thruster at 300 V and 5.4 A, which solves eleven coupled plasma fields and assimilates 145 internal probe measurements per field reconstructed from the data of Haas and Gallimore. The electric potential is obtained from Poisson's equation in charge-separation form, n_e = n_i(1+eta), with eta bounded by construction, which keeps the stiff electrostatic constraint active and trainable. The reference solution agrees with the training profiles to relative L2 errors of 0.017, 0.073 and 0.205 for the potential, electron temperature and ion density, and held-out tests show the potential to be far more robust than the ion density to the withdrawal of measurement lines. We then test the solution against requirements the data fit does not reveal: global particle and current balances, the electron current implied by the momentum equation, the field-aligned electron force balance and the axial ion momentum budget. These expose a neutral inflow six times the measured flow, a bound in the potential representation, and a momentum-implied electron current, more than 99% field-aligned, exceeding the discharge current by orders of magnitude. Correcting these, with a divergence-free magnetic field fitted to measured data, uncertainty-weighted data, the electron pressure gradient and progressively imposed field-aligned and current constraints, yields a solution that conserves particles to within 3%, holds the current between 5.1 and 5.4 A and places 97% of the potential and 88% of the temperature measurements within their uncertainties. Within the tested single-velocity fluid formulation, however, the ion density, potential and ion velocity could not be matched together, and the field-aligned electron balance remains the main obstacle to electron self-consistency.

title: Dynamics of Vortex Electrons in a Uniform Magnetic Field Across Nonrelativistic and Relativistic Regimes
abstract: The dynamics of a vortex electron in a transverse uniform magnetic field involves not only the cyclotron motion of the wave packet center but also the evolution of its internal wavefunction structure. To study this process, we develop a quantum framework and investigate the dynamics of vortex electrons in both the nonrelativistic and relativistic regimes. A discrete Bessel-Gaussian initial wave packet is expanded in the basis of Dirac eigenstates to obtain the time-dependent wavefunction and to analyze its spatiotemporal evolution. In the nonrelativistic regime, the results deviate significantly from the rigid point-dipole model, as the intrinsic kinetic orbital angular momentum exhibits dynamics more complex than simple Larmor precession, owing to the nonstationary internal current distribution of the wave packet. In the relativistic regime, the nonlinear dependence of the energy levels on the quantum numbers destroys the equal spacing of the spectrum. Consequently, the relative phases among the eigenstate components of the wave packet evolve nonuniformly, resulting in wave-packet spreading and deformation, accompanied by modified intrinsic orbital angular momentum dynamics. We introduce a dimensionless parameter to quantify this relativistic dephasing, providing an approximate criterion for selecting physical parameters and evolution times to mitigate the resulting wave-packet distortion. These results clarify the limitations of the rigid point-dipole model, highlight the essential role of internal wavefunction structure, and provide theoretical guidance for understanding and manipulating relativistic vortex electrons.

title: Hydrogen Electron Cyclotron Resonance Dissociator Demonstrator for the Project 8 Experiment
abstract: Project 8, a neutrino mass experiment, employs the novel frequency technique of cyclotron radiation emission spectroscopy (CRES) to perform a model independent measurement of neutrino mass via tritium beta decay. Our pioneering experiment will consist of a beamline that dissociates molecular tritium, surface cools atoms through accommodation, evaporatively cools and slows atoms, and traps them in a CRES resonant cavity to advance towards our sensitivity goal of 40 meV/c^2 for our final electron-weighted neutrino mass measurement. We are prototyping an electron cyclotron resonance (ECR) dissociator that uses a tunable 1 kW 2.45 GHz RF generator and electromagnets to ignite a hydrogen plasma in an aluminum resonant cavity. Our ECR source is designed to produce a high atom flux (~10^19 atoms/second) near room temperature. We present the engineering development, gas diagnostics, and spectroscopy data from our hydrogen plasma.

title: On the Electrodynamics of a Non-Contact Inductive Sensor for High-Accuracy Tip Deflection Measurements of Piezoceramic Bending Actuators and its Application for Energy Harvesting Purposes
abstract: Piezoelectric bending actuators provide deflections of several hundred micrometers and are used in electrical and mechanical engineering, acoustics, automation, automotive technology and healthcare. Highly efficient, low-cost piezoceramics offer a wide range of technical solutions. Their highpiezoelectric coefficients enable large strains at low electric field strengths. However, hysteresis, drift and creep impair positioning accuracy. Precise switching and positioning require compensation for these material-related effects, as well as varying mechanical loads and vibrations. A non-contact inductive proximity sensor is therefore combined with high-precision electronic circuit. Within a closed-loop control system, this sensor-actuator arrangement detects disturbances and enables their compensation, allowing highly efficient piezoceramics to be used for high-accuracy positioning. This paper investigates the electrodynamics of a specially developed eddy-current-based proximity sensor suitable for integration into confined spaces. A theoretical description explains its physical operating principle and enables analytical determination of the relative change in inductance as a function of actuator tip deflection. Experimental measurements validate the electrodynamic approach. The paper also considers energy harvesting applications. Measuring tip deflection allows the power dissipated in the piezoelectric transducer to be determined. The sensor system thus provides a basis for investigating and evaluating the performance of piezoelectric energy harvesters.

title: Interstellar and intergalactic medium in the ultraviolet band
abstract: This article presents an overview of key scientific challenges in the astrophysics and astrochemistry of the interstellar and intergalactic media. Addressing many of these challenges will become possible with the Russian space observatory Spektr-UF, which is currently being prepared for launch. The ultraviolet (UV) spectral range is critically important for studying the evolution of the Universe, as it contains fundamental absorption and emission lines of most chemical elements and the most important molecules. These lines make it possible to reliably determine the physical conditions and chemical composition of various astrophysical objects, as well as the characteristics of the processes occurring within them. The article examines the prospects for UV observations across a broad range of scientific problems, from investigating the epoch of helium reionization and the thermal history of the Universe to mapping ongoing star formation in galaxies. Dedicated sections address the study of the chemical evolution of galaxies at intermediate redshifts, the distribution of "hidden" baryons and metals, the small-scale structure of interstellar clouds, the physics of photodissociation regions and protoplanetary disks, and the modeling of UV emission from nebulae surrounding fast-moving pulsars. The high sensitivity and spectral resolution of the Spektr-UF instruments are expected to provide fundamentally new data across all these research areas, filling existing gaps in our understanding of the interstellar and intergalactic media.

title: Stabilization of counter propagating currents by energy conservation in collisions
abstract: Current filamentation generates magnetic fields and shapes electron transport in dense plasmas, where collisions can either suppress or enhance its growth. Here we show that conserving electron kinetic energy in a collisional model can change both the dominant instability and its characteristic wavelength. We develop a linear kinetic theory for drifting, anisotropic electron populations with a relaxation operator that conserves particle number and laboratory-frame kinetic energy while allowing momentum transfer to a stationary ion background. For counterstreaming currents, energy conservation maintains the stabilizing influence of charge separation over a broader range of collision frequencies than a model conserving particle number alone. At intermediate collision rates, the resulting suppression of transverse filamentation allows a nearly aperiodic oblique mode to dominate, reducing the maximum growth rate and shifting the wavelength of the fastest-growing perturbation. Two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations support predicted growth rates of up to more than a magnitude lower than expected without energy conserving collision.

title: Single-pass stochastic cooling for electron microscopy
abstract: Scientific applications of free electrons, such as in electron microscopes and particle accelerators, are limited by the brightness of available electron sources. Accelerators can use phase space cooling to surpass these source limitations, whereas electron microscopes can only rely on particle filtering to increase beam coherence at the cost of reduced brightness. We show that strong electron-light coupling in nanophotonic structures makes it possible to achieve single-pass stochastic cooling inside an electron microscope for a lossless improvement of longitudinal emittance. This approach is laser-free and compatible with normal CW operation of electron microscopes. We derive a fully quantum mechanical model of stochastic cooling valid in the strong coupling regime, finding an analytic asymptotic formula for the optimal cooled energy spread $σ_{E_f}\simeq0.88(\hbarω)^{2/3}σ_{E_0}^{1/3}$, with $\hbar ω$ the cooling photon energy and $σ_{E_0}$ the initial energy spread. Numerical simulations confirm that the energy spread reduction is reflected in an increase in the purity of the electron's quantum state and a reduction of the longitudinal phase space area. Our work paves a path towards even brighter beams for electron microscopy, promising higher image quality, enhanced spectral resolution, and a route to reaching fundamental quantum limits on electron beam phase space area.

title: Real-time virtual circuits for plasma shape control via neural network emulators
abstract: Reliable position and shape control in tokamak plasmas requires accurate real-time regulation of several strongly coupled shape parameters. The control vectors that disentangle these couplings, referred to as \textit{virtual circuits} (VCs), enable independent shape parameter control for a specific Grad--Shafranov (GS) equilibrium. Numerical calculation of VCs is not currently feasible in real time, therefore VCs are usually computed prior to each experiment, using a small number of reference GS equilibria sampled along the desired scenario trajectory, with each VC used to control the plasma within a preset time interval. While effective near the reference equilibrium, this approach can lead to degraded performance as the plasma departs from the reference equilibrium and/or from the desired trajectory, and it complicates the design of robust control strategies for rapidly evolving plasma configurations. In this paper, we construct neural-network-based emulators of plasma shape parameters from which VCs can be derived, to provide the MAST Upgrade (MAST-U) plasma control system with state-aware VCs in real-time. To do this, we develop an extensive library of over a million simulated GS equilibria, covering a substantial portion of the MAST-U operational space. These emulators provide differentiable functions whose gradients can be rapidly computed, enabling the derivation of accurate VCs for real-time shape control. We perform extensive verification of the emulated VCs by testing whether they disentangle the control problem. The neural-network-based approach delivers high accuracy and orthogonality across a diverse range of equilibria. This work establishes the physical validity of emulated VCs as a scalable and general alternative to schedules of precomputed VCs.

title: Fast Self-Triggering and Segment-Fitting of Cosmic Muons with a small-Diameter Monitored Drift Tube Detector
abstract: We present a fast self-triggering and segment-fitting algorithm that identifies cosmic muons and reconstructs their directions using a small-diameter Monitored Drift Tube (sMDT) chamber without an external trigger detector. The muon arrival time is determined using a Legendre-based algorithm combined with coarse- and fine-grid searches. We implement the algorithm in FPGA firmware on an ATLAS MDT miniDAQ board and evaluate its efficiency, resolution, and latency. The results demonstrate standalone sMDT triggering and trigger-level reconstruction of muon directions, providing a solution for chamber commissioning and potentially MDT-based triggers for charged massive stable particle searches at the High Luminosity-LHC.

title: Semi-analytical representation of the Gaunt-modified Landau-Lifshitz equation in a plane wave
abstract: We analyze electron dynamics in a plane electromagnetic wave using the Landau-Lifshitz equation with a quantum radiation reaction correction modelled by a Gaunt factor. In this geometry, the quantum parameter $χ$ depends solely on the lightfront momentum, allowing the modified equation of motion to retain the integrable structure of the classical problem. We derive a semi-analytical solution for the energy evolution and the four-velocity, which reduces to the known classical result in the appropriate limit. The results provide an analytical and deterministic description of semiclassical radiation reaction in plane-wave fields.

title: Dual-Band Mid-Infrared Imaging for Measurement of Fuel Concentration and Temperature in a Supersonic Cavity
abstract: A dual-band mid-infrared absorption imaging method is demonstrated for spatially resolved measurement of ethylene concentration and temperature in a Mach-2 cavity flow. The method used narrowband filters selected to exploit the differing in-band temperature sensitivities of ethylene absorption, together with a broadband infrared source and high-frame-rate mid-wave infrared camera. Temperature-dependent, filter-weighted absorption cross-sections were used to measure two-dimensional ethylene number density and temperature fields. Measurements were obtained for cavity, curtain, and discrete fuel-injection configurations, including cases with the leading edge of a quasi-steady shock near the cavity. Cavity equivalence ratio measurements agreed well with independent extractive measurements and reproduced trends previously observed using hyperspectral imaging. A complementary single-band implementation using a temperature-independent filter provided instantaneous ethylene concentration fields at 100 Hz and revealed intermittent reductions in cavity equivalence ratio associated with plume deflection by the shock train leading edge. The dual-band approach provides quantitative full-field measurements with substantially simpler spectral instrumentation than hyperspectral imaging while retaining flexibility for time-resolved flow measurements.

title: Solar Wind Turbulence Spectra and Correlation Scale from 4 to 50 $r_\odot$: STEREO and PUNCH Observations
abstract: We investigate the radial evolution of solar wind turbulence using remote-sensing brightness observations from the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) and the first science-ready images from the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission. Exploiting the combined wide fields of view of STEREO's COR2 coronagraph (4-9 r_sun) and PUNCH's Wide Field Imager (WFI, 21-50 r_sun), we track the radial evolution of the power spectral density and correlation scale of density fluctuations from 4 to 50 r_sun. Line-of-sight integration systematically steepens the "usual" turbulence scaling laws by a constant offset of about -0.5 across all resolved scales, so that the energy-containing range (nominally k^-1) and the inertial range (nominally k^-5/3) appear as k^-1.5 and k^-2.1, respectively -- consistent with previous synthetic-image simulations. The correlation scale increases with heliocentric distance across the full range of heliodistances probed, in accordance with previous theoretical models and observations at closer distances from the Sun.

title: A combined segmented anode gas ionization chamber and time-of-flight detector for heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis
abstract: A dedicated detector system for heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis at the Tandem Laboratory of Uppsala University is presented. Benefits of combining a time-of-flight measurement with a segmented anode gas ionization chamber are demonstrated. The capability of ion species identification is improved with the present system, compared to that obtained when using a single solid state silicon detector for the full ion energy signal. The system enables separation of light elements, up to Neon, based on atomic number while signals from heavy elements such as molybdenum and tungsten are separated based on mass, to a sample depth on the order of one micrometer. The performance of the system is discussed and a selection of material analysis applications is given. Plasma-facing materials from fusion experiments, in particular metal mirrors, are used as a main example for the discussion. Marker experiments using nitrogen-15 or oxygen-18 are specific cases for which the described improved species separation and sensitivity are required. Resilience to radiation damage and significantly improved energy resolution for heavy elements at low energies are additional benefits of the gas ionization chamber over a solid state detector based system.

title: Structure of energy flux densities in Earth's magnetotail reconnection regions: Bridging simulation and observation
abstract: Magnetic reconnection is important in both space and laboratory contexts because it changes the topology of magnetic fields and converts magnetic energy into particle energies. Establishing where this energy conversion occurs is critical for understanding how reconnection partitions energy. Using a novel machine learning approach based on simulations that explicitly identifies the separatrix regions for the first time, the partition of energy flux densities within the magnetic reconnection site is evaluated through statistical study of magnetotail reconnection events observed in situ. The separatrices are found to have the largest electron energy flux densities, roughly twice those in the exhaust, and Poynting flux densities about four times those in the inflows, whereas typical ion enthalpy flux densities are largest in the exhaust. The separatrices are therefore sites of intense electron and electromagnetic energy transport, although their small thickness means that the exhaust may still carry most of the total energy flux.

title: Impact of Rapid Acceleration on Beam Dynamics in the Rapid-Cycling Synchrotrons of a Muon Collider
abstract: Circular muon colliders offer a promising route to multi-TeV centre-of-mass energies with high luminosity. The baseline design for the high-energy complex includes a chain of four Rapid-Cycling Synchrotrons (RCSs) accelerating the beam from \qty{63}{\GeV} to \qty{5}{\TeV}. The chain combines a conventional synchrotron with three hybrid synchrotrons, which use fixed-field superconducting dipoles and rapidly ramped normal-conducting dipoles. The short muon lifetime (\qty{2.2}{\micro\second} in the rest frame) imposes stringent constraints on the acceleration process: achieving the target luminosity requires a muon survival rate of up to \qty{70}{\percent} throughout the acceleration chain, with the full acceleration completed in approximately \qty{10}{\milli\second}. These demanding acceleration conditions raise several beam-dynamics challenges, investigated in this work. First, the impact of the RF cavity distribution on transverse emittance growth is studied. Second, the mismatch between the discretely increasing beam energy and the continuously ramped fields of the pulsed dipoles and quadrupoles is modelled analytically, and its impact is evaluated through tracking simulations. Finally, the sensitivity of the beam trajectory, optical functions, and emittance growth to magnetic-field ramp jitter is assessed.

title: Track reconstruction with ACTAR TPC: a transfer-reaction use case
abstract: A unified framework for track reconstruction in the ACTAR Time Projection Chamber (ACTAR TPC) is presented, designed to address the specific challenges of direct-reaction and resonance-elastic scattering experiments involving exotic nuclei. The actroot software package enables efficient semi-online analysis by integrating a continuity-based clustering algorithm followed by a modular filtering procedure to reduce noise, delta-electron contamination, and track fragmentation. The software was benchmarked with experimental data taken with a secondary 20O beam delivered by the LISE3 spectrometer at GANIL. The algorithm achieves reconstruction efficiencies exceeding 90% across various event topologies. The system provides accurate particle identification and reaction-point determination, facilitating the extraction of key physical observables. These results demonstrate the framework's suitability for its application to direct reaction experiments in cubic active-target TPCs without magnetic fields.

title: Detachment dynamics and disturbance rejection in the TCV X-Point Target divertor
abstract: The X-Point Target (XPT) is an alternative divertor configuration with a secondary X-point in the divertor leg. We investigate its detachment dynamics and disturbance rejection capacity on the TCV tokamak, comparing it with a long-legged single-null (SN) divertor. We employ a system identification approach using multi-sine perturbations to D$_2$ fuelling in Ohmic L-mode scenarios and to N$_2$ seeding and electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) power in auxiliary-heated L-mode scenarios, using the CIII emission front position as a proxy for the detached state evolution. For D$_2$ fuelling perturbations at 4-31 Hz, the gain of the front response at the secondary X-point is at least a factor of 3 lower than upstream of it, where the response is similar to that of the SN. This indicates that the reduced detachment sensitivity of the secondary X-point in an XPT configuration previously observed in quasi-steady state experiments, extends to control-relevant timescales as an enhanced disturbance rejection capacity. In auxiliary-heated scenarios, the CIII front in the XPT remains nearly stationary near the secondary X-point under N$_2$ seeding and ECRH power perturbations, whereas the CIII front in SN discharges responds strongly. However, due to complex SOL profiles in the region close to the secondary X-point of the XPT configuration, this reduction in CIII front response may not imply disturbance rejection of the detached state as a whole. The enhanced disturbance rejection at the secondary X-point could provide a passive buffer against disturbances, simplifying the task of exhaust controllers to maintain the detached state throughout a discharge cycle.

title: Deposition rate and energy to substrate in chopped and standard HiPIMS: identifying optimal pulse parameters
abstract: High-Power Impulse Magnetron Sputtering (HiPIMS) delivers higher ionisation of the target material at the expense of lower deposition rates than conventional magnetron sputtering. A fine optimisation of the deposition conditions is crucial for specific applications. Chopped or multi-pulse HiPIMS (segmenting pulses into shorter micropulses) has been proposed to enhance the degree of ionisation of the film-forming flux fraction while maintaining the deposition rate. This study investigates how micropulse length and the delay time between segments influence energy flux, deposition rate, and the ionised flux fraction in both chopped and standard HiPIMS. These quantities are evaluated by passive thermal probe, biasable QCM and mass spectrometer measurements at the substrate position. Deposition-averaged and pulse-averaged power is kept constant for all conditions to facilitate meaningful comparison. Results indicate that chopping the HiPIMS pulse consistently leads to higher energy flux and total deposition rate compared to standard HiPIMS at the same total pulse length, primarily due to increased ion flux. In chopped HiPIMS, increasing the delay time between micropulses beyond 30 us simultaneously improved the deposition rate and the ionised flux fraction. In comparison, standard HiPIMS, operated at higher frequencies and shorter pulse lengths, demonstrated similar performance with even higher total energy fluxes, but this can be attributed to a higher fraction of process-gas ions in the flux to the substrate, rather than to an increased ionised flux fraction of the film-forming species.

title: Comparison of models for dynamical structures of solar plasma
abstract: Possible mechanisms of generation of dynamical plasma structures are associated with the Schwarzschild criterion for convective instability and with excess energy (heat, magnetic): due to the superadiabatic temperature gradient, the overheated plasma starts to rise. In the framework of Navier-Stokes MHD equations, the complete system of equations for the full axisymmetric plasma model includes equations for the stream function, the azimuthal velocity component, the density change, the flow function of poloidal magnetic field, and the azimuthal component of the magnetic field. Within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics, the simplest plasma model is applicable to the initial stage of generation of plasma structures. In this case, rigorous analytical solutions are constructed from blocks. Within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics, some intermediate model - the refined model considers rotating plasma at the growth stage. In this case, some unidirectional differential rotation occurs. The full model studies the development of structures as rotating plasma from the very beginning to the highest development stage. The velocity field is adjusted to boundary conditions. Velocity components change in a coordinated manner. The stationary axisymmetric ambient magnetic field and its gradients have little effect on the plasma structure and velocity field. The movement structures for all models are similar. Radial flows converge towards the axis at the bottom, and there is an outflow to the periphery near the top of the plasma structure. The maximum vertical velocity component is reached at the center of the axis. Applications of these models to solar structures, including jets, are discussed.

title: Numerical Study of Two-Frequency Heating in ECR Ion Source
abstract: The two-frequency heating (TFH) method is widely used to improve the performance of electron cyclotron resonance (ECR) ion sources, yet its physical mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. In this work, the TFH regime in the DECRIS-PM ECR ion source is studied numerically using the NAM-ECRIS code. Single-frequency heating at 14.51 GHz (500 W) is compared to two-frequency heating at 14.51 GHz and 13 GHz (450 W + 50 W) at equal total power. It is found that while the global plasma parameters remain largely unchanged, the peak density of highly anisotropic electrons (E > 1 keV, Vperp/Vlong > 10) decreases by ~20% and their distribution broadens radially in the TFH regime. This reduction in electron anisotropy is attributed to the randomizing effect of the lower-frequency wave on electron gyromotion, which suppresses plasma micro-instabilities and leads to improved ion production.

title: Sub-sonic compressible magnetohydrodynamic turbulence I. Alfvénic and fast-magnetosonic injection, amplitude dependence, and compressibility effects
abstract: We investigate how sub-sonic compressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence properties that are relevant for cosmic-ray (CR) transport in the Galaxy are affected by the nature and amplitude of initial fluctuations, and by the plasma compressibility $β$. We perform 3D simulations of decaying compressible ideal-MHD turbulence at $1024^3$ resolution with the PLUTO code. The level of density fluctuations in fully developed turbulence is insensitive to whether this state is reached starting from Alfvénic or fast-magnetosonic perturbations. Fast-magnetosonic injection is characterized by an early phase of rapid shock dissipation, followed by a turbulence-dominated decay with a rate comparable to that of the Alfvénic case. The contribution of fast-magnetosonic fluctuations in fully developed turbulence remains relevant only when the initial injection consists exclusively of fast modes. Large-amplitude turbulence ($δB/B_0>1$) is characterized by a nearly isotropic Kolmogorov or Iroshnikov-Kraichnan spectrum for Alfvénic or fast-magnetosonic injection, respectively. At low amplitudes ($δB/B_0\ll1$), both initial Alfvénic and mixed-wave perturbations lead to strongly anisotropic turbulence with spectra $\propto k_\perp^{-5/3}$ and $\propto k_z^{-2}$ (becoming steeper at $β\gg1$), whereas fast-magnetosonic perturbations produce a turbulent state populated by shocks with a nearly isotropic $k^{-2}$ spectrum. Magnetic-field curvature and mirror structures are strongly sensitive to fluctuation amplitude and plasma $β$. The predicted -2.5 power-law scaling emerges only in the large-amplitude regime at high $β$. This work highlights that features of sub-sonic compressible MHD turbulence that may affect CR transport are sensitive to large-scale conditions and to the plasma $β$. Their effect on CR diffusion and field-line random walk is the object of Paper II.

title: Dynamic Alignment or Angular Persistence?
abstract: Dynamic alignment in magnetohydrodynamic turbulence is commonly inferred from the decrease of an amplitude-weighted average of the mutual angle between Elsässer increments toward smaller separations. That decrease, however, need not imply that the increments themselves rotate toward alignment: large-angle fluctuations can simply lose more amplitude than small-angle ones. We therefore study the joint evolution of increment amplitude and mutual angle using finite-step conditional transition probabilities. In forced incompressible full MHD and in balanced strong-guide-field reduced MHD, we find that, at fixed initial angle, large-amplitude Elsässer-increment pairs undergo smaller angular changes than small-amplitude pairs, including when they begin at large angles. We call this amplitude-dependent angular persistence. Normalized amplitude moments increase toward smaller separation, while stronger amplitude weighting produces progressively smaller angular averages and stronger scale dependence, linking apparent alignment to the intermittent large-amplitude tail. In RMHD, a source-state decomposition of the Politano-Pouquet third-order moment shows that initially large-angle, high-amplitude populations contribute with the sign associated with transfer toward smaller perpendicular scales despite their comparatively small angular changes. Time-resolved full-MHD data reproduce the same amplitude ordering, and the local Elsässer advective term closely tracks the conditional dependence of both angular and amplitude changes on the initial state. These results show that the conventional dynamic-alignment diagnostic reflects the joint statistical evolution of amplitude and angle and, by itself, is not evidence for a cascade-wide dynamical rotation toward alignment.

title: Imaging the Current Distribution in Superconducting Transition-Edge Sensors with Scanning SQUID Microscopy
abstract: Transition-edge sensors (TESs) exploit the resistive transition of a superconductor to detect minute changes in temperature. While significant progress has been made in understanding the temperature- and current-dependent resistive transition in these devices, important aspects of TES behavior under bias remain unresolved. In particular, existing TES models largely neglect spatial variations in the superconducting state and current distribution arising from device geometry and proximity effects associated with the superconducting leads and normal metal features. Using scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy (SSM), we directly image local superconducting properties and transport current in two molybdenum-gold (MoAu) X-ray TES designs. We measure the local diamagnetic response to identify superconducting regions in devices voltage-biased within the transition and the Oersted field generated by the transport current to reconstruct the corresponding current distribution. We observe bias-dependent reconfigurations of the current distribution that track current-induced changes in superconducting regions, highlighting the importance of mesoscale spatial variations for TES device physics, operation, and design.

title: Characteristic Mapping Method for Vlasov-Poisson with BGK-collisions
abstract: This work presents the first steps for simulating kinetic plasmas with collisions using the characteristic mapping method (CMM). The CMM is a semi-Lagrangian method that uses the group structure of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms to efficiently represent the flow-maps of transport problems. Individual submaps can be composed to follow the flow backward in time to its initial foot point, numerically establishing the back-to-label symmetry. The novelty of the presented work is the handling of the source term by storing the Duhamel integrals of each time sub-interval, allowing efficient temporal-integration. Furthermore, we use the Lagrangian structure to avoid implicit time-stepping in the hydrodynamic regime, which is known to be stiff. We benchmark our method on the Boltzmann-BGK and Vlasov-Poisson-BGK equations and consider different test cases, the Sod shock tube problem and nonlinear Landau damping for different Knudsen numbers. We show third-order spatial and temporal convergence and illustrate the fine-scale zoom property of CMM for the bump-on-tail instability.

title: The Birth of Plasmoids: Weibel-Driven Secondary Tearing and its Suppression in Relativistic Reconnection
abstract: Plasmoids, or magnetic islands, dominate relativistic reconnection layers in kinetic simulations, yet the instability that creates them remains poorly understood. By tracking newborn islands in 2D particle-in-cell simulations of pair-plasma reconnection with magnetizations $0.1\leσ_0\le1000$, we show that plasmoids are seeded by a current-filamentation/Weibel instability driven by counter-streaming out-of-plane current carriers near primary x-lines. Measured growth rates are $\sim0.1$ times the background plasma frequency and agree with linear theory evaluated on the simulated distributions. As inflowing plasma loads the sheet away from the x-line, the current is carried by more particles and their out-of-plane drift slows. The filamentation instability shuts off once this drift becomes comparable to the momentum spread in the outflow direction, which occurs at a distance $\ell_{\rm iso}\proptoσ_0$ from the x-line. Because the unstable region extends farther at higher $σ_0$, our results account for the onset of plasmoid-dominated reconnection in the relativistic regime but predict that plasmoid formation is suppressed beyond $\sim\ell_{\rm iso}$ from primary x-lines, even in ultra-relativistic reconnection. Particle acceleration, variability, and coherent radio emission attributed to plasmoid-dominated reconnection may therefore be confined to smaller regions than previously assumed.

title: Feed-forward active magnetic shielding
abstract: Measurement of small magnetic fields requires shielding. For example, magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures small fields arising within the brain, in the presence of environmental fields several orders of magnitude larger. A common solution is passive shielding, but its cost, bulk and limited effectiveness motivate the alternative approach of active shielding, which comes in two flavours: feed-back and feed-forward. In feed-back shielding (the most common design), coils are driven from sensors that measure the corrected field. In feed-forward shielding (less common), coils are driven from sensors that measure the uncorrected field. The latter has the potential of providing better performance, but its implementation is hobbled by an inevitable coupling between coils and reference sensors. This paper describes an approach that employs a data-driven ``decoupling matrix" to suppress the coupling, enabling greater flexibility to achieve effective shielding across a wide frequency range. The method is evaluated by simulation, first using a simplified "flat world" in which the principle is clearly visualised, and then based on the more realistic geometry of a standard MEG system. Performance appears to be limited only by spatial sampling and numerical resolution. The method, which is data-driven and does not require geometric calculations, tight-tolerance fabrication, or manual calibration, is complementary with standard feed-back shielding methods. Active shielding is of particular interest in the context of a new generation of optically-pumped magnetometers (OPM), as the lower cost and reduced constraints of these new systems relative to SQUID-based systems provide an incentive to likewise reduce the cost and constraints of shielding.

title: Computational studies of giant edge islands and unpaired X-points in HSX and W7-X by manipulating coil currents
abstract: We present magnetic configurations in the Helically Symmetric eXperiment (HSX) and Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X), in which the edge magnetic structure exhibits island chains which are spatially larger than the previously reported configurations. These ``giant" island chains (with rotational transform $ι=4/3$ or $4/4$ for HSX and $ι=5/6$, $5/5$ or $5/4$ for W7-X) are obtained by reducing the coil current in main coil 6 for HSX and non-planar coil 5 for W7-X (i.e. the coil nearest the up-down symmetric cross-section $φ=36^\circ$ for W7-X and $φ=45^\circ$ for HSX). This appears a sufficient (but not necessary) condition for giant islands. The giant islands create X-point legs which transport plasma to the plasma-facing components (PFCs). In the most extreme cases, the island O-points leave the domain of the field line map and the divertor legs of the remaining ``unpaired" X-points do not close around the island. We show for W7-X, via the construction of quadratic flux-minimising surfaces, that these island size trends can mostly be interpreted as changes in magnitude of a resonant perturbation on a changing resonant ``unperturbed" magnetic surface. We use the anisotropic heat diffusion code EMC3-Lite to find ``giant island" W7-X configurations which are promising for PFC heat loads. These configurations significantly degrade the neoclassical transport performance but allow exploration of novel divertor regimes; for example, we show that the internal island pitch can be increased. This leads to favourable downstream/upstream plasma density ratios according to simple models; an attractive finding which motivates further investigation.

title: SensOFormer: Foundation Models for Particle Accelerators
abstract: Large-scale scientific facilities, such as particle accelerators, are complex systems composed of thousands of interacting components that must operate collectively to support diagnostics and control, and ensure safe, reliable operation. These facilities rely on extensive sensor networks that generate large volumes of heterogeneous, incomplete, and noisy telemetry, often sampled at different rates across subsystems. In this paper, we adopt the foundation-model paradigm to learn general-purpose sensor representations from historical accelerator data through self-supervised pretraining. We introduce SensOFormer, a denoising masked transformer with a Perceiver-style encoder-decoder architecture designed to handle variable sensor sets, accommodate heterogeneous sampling rates, and learn robust representations from noisy measurements. The model is pretrained on multiple particle-accelerator datasets and transferred to downstream tasks, including missing-data imputation, anomaly detection, cavity identification, and fault identification. Through extensive evaluations and comparisons, we demonstrate that a single self-supervised model can learn reusable representations for diverse operational tasks in large-scale scientific facilities. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/sensoformer.

title: Detecting Muons with a Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra
abstract: Atmospheric muons are routinely detected with a variety of instruments, from cloud chambers to scintillation detectors. In this study, we demonstrate that atmospheric muons can also be detected with a clinical long axial field-of-view positron emission tomograph (PET). We performed a blank scan without any radioactive source, using a prototype feature that records all single crystal interactions. The energy a muon deposits in the PET crystals far exceeds the upper limit of the recorded energy range, which means muons cannot be identified through energy discrimination. Instead, we used the scanner's time-of-flight capabilities to select crossing events, i.e. pairs of high-energy single crystal events across the PET gantry whose spatial and temporal separation is consistent with a downward-going ultrarelativistic particle. Random pairings, however, cannot be rejected on an event-by-event basis. We therefore established the muon origin of the crossing events through their characteristic angular distribution. In order to account for geometry and event selection bias, we compare the measured crossing events to a Monte Carlo simulation of muons following the expected angular distribution. This confirms that the measured crossing events in the PET scanner are consistent with atmospheric muons.

title: Cryogenic performance of Silicon Photo-Multipliers at LN$_2$ temperature and at 3 K in the RES-NOVA cryostat
abstract: Silicon Photo-Multipliers (SiPMs) are semiconductor-based photodetectors that offer performance comparable to that of traditional Photo-Multiplier Tubes (PMTs), while providing several advantages, including low operating voltage, immunity to magnetic fields, compact size, and mechanical robustness. These features have led to their widespread adoption in scintillator-based detectors for both fundamental and applied physics. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the detection of scintillation light at cryogenic temperatures in low-temperature experiments based on bolometric detectors, such as RES-NOVA and CUPID, as well as in emerging quantum applications. In the RES-NOVA experiment, radiopure PbWO$_4$ crystals are used to detect supernova neutrinos. The scintillation of PbWO$_4$ can only be evaluated at cryogenic temperatures, as the scintillation light yield is negligible at room temperature. We present measurements of the performance at cryogenic temperatures of Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS SiPMs in terms of breakdown voltage and gain, at 77~K (in a liquid nitrogen bath) and at 3~K. The cooling down to 3~K has been carried out using a Proteox LX cryostat from Oxford Instruments.

title: Influence of the Coulomb Interaction on the Radiation of a Few Body System
abstract: Understanding energy absorption in laser-plasma interactions is crucial for applications ranging from inertial confinement fusion to particle acceleration. At the most fundamental level, this energy exchange is governed by the motion of individual charged particles in the laser field. However, when multiple particles are present, their mutual Coulomb interaction can modify the dynamics and, consequently, the energy absorption. In this work, we investigate this scenario by solving the classical equations of motion for two coupled charged particles interacting with an intense laser field. Within the plasma approximation, we find that the Coulomb interaction between the electrons does not significantly affect the energy transfer during the laser-matter interaction. Additionally, we explore the role of mass asymmetry by considering the classical electron-proton interaction as a target system. Our results highlight the critical importance of mass: the proton, due to its much slower dynamics, acquires substantially less energy from the field compared to the electron, leading to a pronounced asymmetry in the energy distribution between the two species.

title: Cryogenic Optoelectronic Characterization of InGaAsP LEDs for Low-Energy Detector Calibration
abstract: We measured the emission spectra and current-voltage (IV) characteristics of commercial InGaAsP LEDs in a cryostat over a temperature range from 7 K to 300 K. At a constant operating current of 3.3 mA, the peak emission wavelength of the 1200 nm (1650 nm) LED decreased from 1202.3 +/- 0.5 nm (1665.5 +/- 0.6 nm) at 300 K to 1143.1 +/- 0.3 nm (1539.5 +/- 2.2 nm) at 7 K, demonstrating a strong temperature dependence. The cut-in voltage increased systematically with decreasing temperature, in agreement with conventional diode theory. To assess junction self-heating effects, we conducted pulsed IV measurements at different duty cycles. The extracted apparent series resistance showed a clear duty-cycle dependence, whereas the cut-in voltage remained unchanged within experimental uncertainty, indicating that self-heating primarily influenced the IV slope rather than the cut-in voltage. These results quantitatively characterize the thermal behavior of both the spectral peak and key electrical parameters, supporting the application of InGaAsP LEDs as cryogenic calibration light sources.
